R01.note: Explains the cost of throwing ordinary errors while acknowledging that handwritten validation can return the same 400 and must accept null.

errors: "The only error that becomes a 400" extends the verified behavior beyond the specified thrown Error cases.
"persistent retry flood" and effects on "any handler side effects that already ran" are not established by the facts.
"every guest-checkout webhook" overstates customer nullability, which applies to some event types.
"your existing clients get the error shape they already handle" invents client behavior.
"throwing a ZodError-shaped error" is not established as sufficient for middleware that catches ZodError.
"you've built a worse zod" is an unsupported judgment.
R02.note: The concrete status-code explanation is buried under invented consequences and an unnecessarily restricted account of handwritten alternatives.

errors: "the logs show which path failed" is not established.
"Stripe keeps resending it for 3 days" turns an upper limit into a fixed duration.
"pushes past 5 per minute" assumes an unverified delivery rate.
"it's now a second 400 format, different" assumes handwritten validation cannot reproduce the existing response.
"nothing new" and "no added ... bundle size" overstate what having an existing dependency proves.
"about the same length as three typeof checks" is an unverified code-size comparison.
"lost without anyone noticing" assumes an absence of monitoring or other recovery.
R03.note: It introduces the relevant machinery well but repeats the argument and treats several possible consequences as inevitable.

errors: "the other 14 routes would behave differently from this one" assumes handwritten validation would return a different response.
"retry for 3 days" replaces the verified maximum with a fixed duration.
"dropped silently" assumes no visibility into rejected deliveries.
"about the same length as the hand-rolled version" compares against an implementation that has not been shown.
R04.note: It gives a clear failure-path explanation and usable nullable schema, but exaggerates differences that handwritten validation could avoid.

errors: "Hand-rolled checks ... so a bad body would fall through as a 500" assumes the checks throw an ordinary Error rather than return 400.
R05.note: It is concise, but leads with a convention label and omits the condition under which handwritten validation actually causes a 500.

errors: "it's less code to get that behavior" is a plausible inference presented without a demonstrated implementation comparison.
R06.note: It answers the objection directly and preserves the viable handwritten option, though it leaves the paging threshold and response shape unspecified.

errors: "saves about a dozen lines" invents a numerical comparison.
"puts the endpoint on the error path that 500s" assumes handwritten validation throws ordinary errors.
"three days of repeated deliveries" treats the retry maximum as a guaranteed duration.
"any client-side handling ... sees two shapes" assumes response-format divergence and client behavior.
"adds no measurable per-request work" is unsupported by measurements.
"ZodError is the only thing ... turns into a 400; anything else is a 500" exceeds the verified claim about other thrown Errors.
R07.note: It repeats a useful error-path argument while adding unsupported measurements, client behavior, and distracting markup.

errors: "A hand-written check would throw a plain Error" assumes an implementation choice.
"Zod costs nothing extra here" overstates the established fact that no new dependency is needed.
"we'd silently lose those events" assumes no visibility or recovery beyond automatic retries.
R08.note: It explains the operational consequences and supplies the corrected schema, but presents avoidable handwritten behavior as the default certainty.

errors: "fine only if it returns 400 itself" excludes other possible ways to use recognized errors or shared response handling.
"every guest-checkout event" overstates the documented null case.
"resend each one for 3 days" turns an upper limit into a guaranteed duration.
"Stripe ignores the body of a webhook response" is not among the verified facts.
"using it adds nothing" overstates what an existing dependency proves.
"Neither choice saves effort" asserts an unverified implementation comparison.
R09.note: The missing-parent TypeError example makes the risk tangible, but unsupported Stripe behavior and effort claims weaken the judgment.

errors: "a guest-checkout event gets 400" also covers handwritten rejection, whose status depends on how it reports failure.
"that order never reaches billing" invents an order-processing consequence and rules out unverified recovery paths.
"errors.ts only maps ZodError to 400" extends the verified behavior beyond the specified thrown Error cases.
R10.note: It clearly conditions the main handwritten-error risk, but invents a billing outcome and opens with the same convention-based justification the user challenged.
